lesson.title: Count what can happen

lead.text: Start with the smallest case. Flip a coin twice and write down what you see, using H for heads and T for tails. The first flip can be H or T, and whichever it is, the second flip can be H or T as well. Written in order, the possible results are HH, HT, TH and TT. HT means heads on the first flip and tails on the second, so it is a different result from TH.

Each of those four results is an outcome: one complete way for the flips to turn out. A group of outcomes you care about is an event. “At least one head” is an event, and it holds three outcomes, HH, HT and TH.

Suppose the coin is fair, so that no outcome is favoured over another. The outcomes are then equally likely, and the chance of an event is its share of the list. Three of the four outcomes are in our event, so the probability of at least one head is 3 out of 4. Whenever every outcome is equally likely, the probability of an event is the number of outcomes in it divided by the number of outcomes altogether.
That sentence is the method for the whole lesson. The only hard part is the counting, and the rest of the lesson is about counting when the list is too long to write out.
Try the same method on a different event with the same two coins. List the outcomes first, then count the ones that match.

Coins give a list short enough to write on one line. Dice do not. Roll one die and then another, and the first can show any of six numbers, with the second free to show any of six after it. Writing every pair out would be slow, so we draw a grid: the first roll runs down the side and the second runs along the top, so each cell holds one pair.

Order matters. A 1 on the first die and a 6 on the second is the cell (1,6). A 6 first and a 1 second is the cell (6,1), which sits somewhere else in the grid. Both are outcomes, and every cell is as likely as any other, because each die is fair.

afterFigure.text: The shaded cells in the picture are the pairs that add up to 7. We come back to them shortly. For now the useful fact is the shape of the grid. It always has one row for each face of the first die and one column for each face of the second, so dice with a different number of faces make a grid of a different size. Count along a row and down a column, and you know how many outcomes there are.

lead.text: Each cell of the grid is one ordered outcome. Look at how the grid is built before you answer.

reveal.text: Six rows of six cells. (1,6) and (6,1) sit in different cells, so both are counted.

lead.text: Now we can use the grid. The shaded cells are the pairs that add up to 7, running along the diagonal from (1,6) to (6,1). There are six of them, and every cell is equally likely. The chance of a total of 7 is the shaded share of the grid: 6 out of 36, which simplifies to 1 in 6.

Compare a total of 2. Only one pair makes it, the double (1,1), so its share is 1 out of 36. The list of possible totals runs neatly from 2 to 12, and it is tempting to think each total is as likely as the next. They are not. A total gets its chance from the number of cells that lead to it, and the totals in the middle have the most cells.

afterFigure.text: Move the total on the picture and watch the shaded cells grow towards 7 and shrink again after it. That pattern is why 7 is the favourite in every dice game.

lead.text: Compare the corner of the grid, where both dice show 1, with the shaded diagonal.

steps.headline: Find the probability that two dice total 8.

workedSteps.text: Go along the first rolls and find the partner each one needs. A first roll of 2 needs a 6, and a first roll of 3 needs a 5.
Count all the pairs that make 8.

lead.text: So far an event has been a single total. An event can also gather several totals. “A total of at least 11” means 11 or 12, and every pair that reaches either of them belongs to the event.

The counting goes the same way as before: add up the cells for each total in the event. A total of 11 has two cells, (5,6) and (6,5), and a total of 12 has one, (6,6). Together that is 3 cells, so the probability is 3 out of 36, which is 1 in 12.

afterFigure.text: The bottom of the fraction stays the whole grid, whatever the event is. Each cell has one total, so no cell can be counted twice. Move the total on the picture to see how the event grows as the limit comes down.

lead.text: An event can hold several totals. Count the cells for every total in it, then divide by the cells in the whole grid.

Every cell in the grid is either inside an event or outside it. Take “a total of at least 11” again. Its 3 cells are inside, and the other 33 cells are outside. The two groups share no cell, and together they fill the grid.

That gives a shortcut. The probability of the cells outside an event is 33 out of 36, and it equals 1 minus the probability of the event, because 1 stands for the whole grid. What an event leaves out is called its complement. When an event is large, counting its complement is often quicker than counting the event itself.
The question below asks about a total under 10, which is the complement of a total of at least 10. Questions that say “not” are often complements too.
Every pair either makes at least 10 or does not. No pair is in both groups, and together the two groups fill the grid.

reveal.text: You did not recount the grid. The cells outside the event are its complement, and the two probabilities add to 1.

lesson.orientation: Use equally likely ordered outcomes to calculate a probability, and avoid treating possible sums as equally likely.
lesson.nextAction: Try a new case and return for recall after a delay.

blocks.text: Pick up almost any board game and you will find two dice in the box. You shake them and let go, and everyone leans in to see the total. After a few games you start to notice something. A 7 turns up all the time, and a 2 hardly ever does. Players who have never studied chance plan around that, and they are right to.

The feeling can be made exact. A fair die has no memory and no favourites, so what two dice do on any throw is a matter of counting. If you can list everything the dice might show, you can say how often each total will come up, and you can say it before the dice leave your hand.
This lesson does the listing. It begins with two coins, because a list of four things is easy to hold in your head. Then it moves to two dice, where the list grows into a grid of pairs.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the chance of a dice total by counting, and see why 7 turns up more often than 2.

recap.keyIdea: When outcomes are equally likely, a probability is the number of outcomes in the event divided by the number of all outcomes.

blocks.text: You began with two coins and four outcomes, then built a grid for two dice. Six of its cells make a total of 7 and only one makes a 2, which is why 7 comes up so often. You counted 6 cells for at least 10 and found the other 30 by taking the complement.

recap.nextHook: That grid assumes you know nothing about the throw. When a friend glimpses one die and tells you something about it, part of the grid is no longer possible. The next lesson starts from there.

questions.prompt: Roll two fair dice, one after the other. How many ordered outcomes are possible?
hints: Count the rows, then the cells in each row.
Each first-roll value can pair with every second-roll value.
Multiply the number of first-roll choices by the number of second-roll choices.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 6 first rolls and 6 second rolls, giving 6 × 6 = 36 ordered outcomes.

questions.onCorrect: 36. Each of the 6 first rolls pairs with all 6 second rolls, so you multiply.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two dice. Each first roll pairs with every second roll, so the counts combine another way.
That is one die. The grid lists both rolls together, one cell per pair.

questions.prompt: Only (1,1) makes a total of 2. Why is a total of 7 more likely?
hints: Compare how many cells match each total.

acceptedIdeas: More ordered pairs make 7 than make 2
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Six equally likely ordered pairs total 7, whereas only (1, 1) totals 2. Probabilities depend on the number of matching pairs, not just the list of possible sums.

choices.label: Every possible sum is equally likely
More ordered pairs make 7 than make 2
The second die always makes large totals

questions.onCorrect: Six pairs make 7 and one makes 2. Totals with more pairs are more likely.

misconceptions.feedback: Count the cells for each total. If every sum were equally likely, the cell counts would match.
Neither die favours big numbers. Look at how many pairs reach each total.

questions.prompt: What is the probability that the total is at least 10? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Count only matching pairs, then divide by all 36 pairs.
List the pairs for totals 10, 11 and 12, including reversed pairs.
There are three pairs for 10, two for 11 and one for 12; divide their combined count by the full grid count.
questions.onCorrect: Six of 36: 3 + 2 + 1 pairs for 10, 11 and 12. The denominator stays every pair.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of pairs. A probability divides it by all the pairs.
That counts totals, not pairs. Totals are not equally likely, so count cells.

questions.prompt: So what is the probability that the total is below 10? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Subtract the probability of at least 10 from 1.
The events below 10 and at least 10 partition the full grid.
Subtract the six pairs at least 10 from the full count, then divide by the full count.
questions.onCorrect: Leave out the 6 pairs: 30 of 36. The complement is everything the event is not.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the probability of at least 10. This question asks about the pairs that are left.
That is a count of pairs. A probability divides by all the pairs.

questions.prompt: Two fair four-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the total is 5? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: List the pairs that sum to 5; the changed dice have four sides each.
The pairs (1,4) and (4,1) are distinct; include both middle pairs too.
Divide the four matching pairs by four first choices times four second choices.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four pairs make 5: (1,4), (2,3), (3,2), (4,1). There are 16 pairs, so 4/16 = 1/4.

questions.onCorrect: Four of 16 pairs: the grid is 4 × 4 now, and (1,4) and (4,1) count separately.

misconceptions.feedback: Check whether (1,4) and (4,1) are being counted as one pair. They are different outcomes.
36 belongs to six-sided dice. How many pairs do two four-sided dice make?

questions.prompt: When may you calculate probability by counting favourable outcomes over all outcomes?
hints: Counting gives each outcome the same weight.

acceptedIdeas: Whenever the outcomes are equally likely
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The favourable-count divided by total-count shortcut requires equally likely outcomes. If their probabilities differ, add the probabilities of the favourable outcomes instead.

choices.label: Whenever the outcomes are equally likely
Only when the event is certain

questions.onCorrect: Counting favourable over all outcomes needs every outcome equally likely.

misconceptions.feedback: The names of the outcomes do not matter. What matters is whether each has the same chance.
Counting works for uncertain events too. The condition is about the outcomes' chances.

questions.prompt: A coin is flipped twice. HT means heads, then tails. How many different results can you get, counting HT and TH as different?
hints: Write them out: start with the ones that begin with heads.
Two begin with H. How many begin with T?
List HH, HT, then the two that begin with T.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: HH, HT, TH and TT: 4 results.

questions.onCorrect: 4: HH, HT, TH, TT. Listing every result is where probability starts.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts how many heads you might see: none, one or two. HT and TH are different results, so list the order too.
Each flip has two sides, but the flips go together. List what the pair of flips can show.

questions.prompt: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the total is not 12? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: How many of the 36 pairs make a total of 12?
Only one pair makes 12. How many pairs are left over?
Count the pairs that are not 12, then divide by all the pairs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only (6,6) makes 12, so 36 − 1 = 35 pairs do not: 35/36.

questions.onCorrect: 35/36. Count what the event leaves out, then divide by every pair: the complement.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the probability of a total of 12. The question asks about every other pair.
That treats the eleven possible totals as equally likely. Count pairs instead: some totals have more than one.

questions.prompt: How many ordered pairs make a total of 8?
hints: Start with a first roll of 2. What second roll makes 8?
Work along the first rolls. Does a first roll of 1 have a partner?
The pairs run (2,6) to (6,2). Count them.
questions.onCorrect: 5 pairs. Each first roll from 2 to 6 has exactly one partner.

misconceptions.feedback: A first roll of 1 would need a second roll of 7. Check which first rolls have a partner.
Count (4,4) too, and keep both (2,6) and (6,2).

questions.prompt: What is the probability that the total is 8? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Use the count you just made.
Divide the pairs that make 8 by all the pairs.
Your count goes on top; the bottom is every ordered pair.
questions.onCorrect: 5/36. Pairs that make 8, over every equally likely pair.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 6 ÷ 36. Use the number of pairs that make 8, not 6.
That treats the eleven possible totals as equally likely. Divide by the number of pairs.

questions.prompt: Two coins are flipped. What is the probability of exactly one head? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: List all four results.
Which of the four results have exactly one head?
Put the number of those results over the number of all results.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: HT and TH are 2 of the 4 results: 2/4.

questions.onCorrect: Exactly one head holds two of the four outcomes. Count the event, divide by all.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts one outcome. The event holds more than one.
TT is a result too. Count every equally likely result, not just the ones with heads.

citations.claim: An outcome is one result, an event is a group of outcomes, and counting outcomes needs them equally likely.
Two coin flips have four equally likely ordered results, and exactly one head holds two of them.
Two dice give a grid of ordered outcomes, one cell per pair of rolls.
Two dice give a grid of ordered outcomes, one cell per pair of rolls.
A probability is the number of pairs in the event over all equally likely pairs; six pairs make 7 and one makes 2.
More ordered pairs make 7 than make 2, so totals are not equally likely.
Five pairs make a total of 8, so the probability is 5/36.
An event can collect several totals; at least 11 has 3 pairs of 36.
An event can collect several totals; at least 10 has 6 pairs of 36.
An event and its complement fill the grid without overlap, so their probabilities add to 1.
An event and its complement fill the grid without overlap.
Two dice give 6 × 6 = 36 ordered outcomes.
More ordered pairs make 7 than make 2.
Totals 10, 11 and 12 have 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 outcomes; 6/36 = 1/6.
The complement has 36 − 6 = 30 outcomes, so 30/36 = 5/6.
Four of the 16 pairs make 5 on two four-sided dice: 1/4.
Counting favourable over all outcomes needs equally likely outcomes.
Only (6,6) makes 12, so 35 of 36 pairs do not.
Five pairs make a total of 8.
Five of 36 pairs make 8: 5/36.
An event of two outcomes out of four equally likely ones has probability 2/4.
The pairs (1,2) and (2,1) give 3, so the probability is 2/36 = 1/18.
The complement of A consists of the outcomes where A does not occur.
